headline: Kanshin is 関 (kan, “concern”) plus 心 (shin, “heart”).
Hakase is ultimately from Middle Chinese 博士, an official title in the ritsuryō system, likely borrowed in the Old Japanese period.
Kōsha is 校 (kō, “school”) plus 舎 (-sha, “house”), first attested in 1884.
Ke, “hair”, is cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *ke (“hair, fur”).
Kangofu is 看護 (“nursing”) plus 婦 (“woman; female”).
Chōsa is chō (調, investigate) plus sa (査, look into).
Sore is そ (so, “that”, medial reference marker) plus れ (-re, specific pronoun referent marker).
Yane is 屋 (ya, “building, house”) plus 根 (ne, “root”), and ancient houses were dugouts where the roof came right down to the ground.
Chigai is the continuative stem of 違う (chigau, “to differ”).
Tōri is the stem form of 通る (tōru, “to go by; to go past; to go along”).
Sekidō is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 赤道 (chìdào).
Kurushimu is first cited to the Kojiki of 712 CE, related to 苦しい (kurushii, “painful, suffering”).
Butsu is a shift from 打つ (utsu).
Kakeru, “to bet”, is derived from 掛ける (kakeru, “to hang; to manipulate; to spend, invest”).
Atsukamashii is related to 厚い (atsui, “thick”).
Setsubi appears to be a Meiji-period repurposing of written Chinese 設備 (shèbèi, “equipment; to make preparations”) and Old Japanese 設け備ふ (makesonapu).
Nichiyōhin is, by surface analysis, 日用 (nichiyō, “everyday use”) plus 品 (-hin, “item”).
Tsukamu is derived from 束 (tsuka, “bunch, bundle”) plus -mu, and is first cited to a text from 850.
Kurīmu is English cream, a doublet of クレーム (kurēmu).
Jidōsha is 自動 (jidō, “automatic movement”) plus 車 (-sha, “vehicle”).
Geijutsu is from Literary Chinese 藝術, collectively the 六藝 (Liùyì, “Six Arts”) and 術數 (shùshù, “numerology”).
Taira is た (ta-) plus 平 (hira), attested in the Nihon Shoki (720 CE).
Ashiato is 足 (ashi, “foot”) plus 跡 (ato, “trace, mark”).
Nagai is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, and is possibly cognate with 流れる (nagareru, “to flow”), in reference to extending.
Setsu, “theory”, is from Middle Chinese 說.
Kinzoku is Middle Chinese 金屬, literally “metal + be attached to; category”.
Zairyō is a Middle Chinese compound, literally “materials + ingredients”.
Botchan is 坊 (bō) plus ちゃん (-chan).
Kado, “corner”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kanto.
Irasshai is the imperative of いらっしゃる (irassharu), shortened from いらっしゃいまし (irasshaimashi).
Shōka is from Middle Chinese 消化 (MC sjew xwaeH).
